prize_parts.citation: for the prediction of flat bands at magic twist angles in twisted bilayer graphene and the experimental discovery of correlated insulating and superconducting states there

statement.case_for: I keep magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene as my single-part preference, and round 1 has sharpened rather than weakened the reasons. What I value is a simple, general mechanism that can be written down analytically and then tested: the 2011 Bistritzer-MacDonald continuum model shows that a long-wavelength moire potential quenches the kinetic energy at a discrete set of twist angles, and the 2018 experiments found correlated insulators and superconductivity at the angle the model singled out. Several colleagues (Danielsson, Olsson, Eriksson) have supplied the distinction I wanted: the secure content is the flat bands plus the reproduced phase diagram, and the open pairing glue belongs to the field that the prize would open. The mechanism has travelled to many van der Waals systems, which is what separates a platform from a single material. The names are also stable: all eight members' positions using B009 or alternatives accept the same three, and nobody wants to split Bistritzer from MacDonald. The citation I propose rests on flat bands at magic angles and the observed correlated and superconducting states, and deliberately makes no claim about the pairing mechanism.
statement.case_against: The reservation I take most seriously is attribution and the sharpness of what is being credited. Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto identified a reduced Fermi velocity and flat-band tendencies in twisted bilayers earlier, and the 2018 experiments were carried out by a team whose first authors (Cao, Fatemi and others) are outside a three-name limit; Cory Dean's group is also relevant. The pairing mechanism is open and twist-angle disorder makes some claims soft, which is a real maturity cost against the optical lattice clock, where independent laboratories agree to about 1e-18. If the committee judged that the primary literature does not support putting the quantitative magic-angle statement with Bistritzer-MacDonald, or that the experimental credit cannot be drawn defensibly, I would regard B049 as the more defensible choice and not insist on B009.

responses.point: Johansson prefers the optical lattice clock (Katori, Ye) as a discovery-level change in what can be measured, ranks twisted bilayer graphene lower because the superconductivity is unsettled, and still lists B009 as an alternative; in round 1 he also said he would not press active matter without more evidence of robustness.
responses.response: I accept his criticism of active matter and have dropped it from my alternatives; he and Pearce were right that I could not name a decisive measurement of the Toner-Tu exponents that the committee could cite. On the maturity point we now agree on the facts and differ on the weight. The pairing glue is open, but the flat bands, the correlated insulator and the superconducting dome have been reproduced by many groups, so a citation worded around those states does not depend on the glue, in the same way that recognition of quantum Hall physics did not wait for every question about the fractional states. Where I partly move toward him is the clock: Katori's magic wavelength is a conceptual step and not just a refinement, because it resolves the trade-off between many atoms and perturbation of the transition. My remaining question is the one he himself leaves unverified, namely whether this is a new phenomenon or the third prize in one metrology lineage, and I cannot settle that from memory. That is why B049 is now my first alternative.

responses.point: Lindroth argues that the lattice clock is a real conceptual step, with Katori's idea and Ye's demonstration of 1e-18 performance, and that agreement among independent laboratories is the robustness she looks for; she names novelty relative to the 2005 and 2012 prizes as the strongest objection.
responses.response: This is the most persuasive account of the clock on the table, and as a non-specialist in atomic physics I defer to her on the physics of trapping many neutral atoms Doppler- and recoil-free. I would put the same question to her that she puts to the graphene case: is repeated quantitative theory-experiment comparison, with blackbody and higher-order lattice shifts calculated and then checked, a sufficient answer to the lineage objection? I think it is a good answer, and it is why I now list B049 first among alternatives. What keeps me at B009 is a difference of kind and not of quality: the clock sharpens a measurement we already knew how to make, whereas moire flat bands revealed a route to strong correlations nobody had expected, and I put somewhat more weight on that discovery element. I recognise this is a judgment about prize philosophy that she can reasonably reject.

responses.point: Olsson argues that Lopes dos Santos found a reduced Fermi velocity at small angles whereas Bistritzer-MacDonald predicted flat bands at specific magic angles, the part the experiment tested, and asks the committee to check this against the primary literature.
responses.response: Her distinction is the one I was looking for and it improves the citation: the Bistritzer-MacDonald contribution is the quantitative continuum model with a specific magic angle, which is what the experiment tested, while earlier work established the tendency and not the discrete flat-band condition. I take her point that none of us should rely on memory, so I state the claim as a premise to be checked and not as a settled fact. I also agree with her on the fractional Chern insulator: it is a downstream consequence of the platform and argues for patience on a later prize, not for withholding this one. On her experimental-credit concern I have no clean answer: three names mean Cao, Fatemi and others go uncredited, and I would say so openly rather than hide it.

responses.point: Danielsson argues that waiting for the fractional Chern insulator risks losing the chance to credit the founders while the field is young, and that the 2011 prediction plus the 2018 experiment is exactly what the citation describes.
responses.response: I agree and withdraw my earlier suggestion that a later moire result might be the more stable thing to recognise. The risk he names is real: the prediction and the original experiment are what the field rests on, and a more elegant later result would not displace them. I do not agree that attribution is fully settled; I would keep the citation limited to the magic-angle prediction and the 2018 states, and say that nothing in it claims the earliest observation of flattening bands.

uncertainties: Whether the primary literature supports the quantitative magic-angle statement being credited to Bistritzer-MacDonald and not to the earlier work of Lopes dos Santos, Peres and Castro Neto; I am relying on memory and colleagues' accounts.
Whether leaving out Cao, Fatemi and other experimental co-first authors, and Cory Dean's group, is defensible within a three-name limit.
Whether the open pairing mechanism and twist-angle disorder make the superconductivity part of the citation premature, so that correlated insulators and flat bands should carry the weight.

Whether a measurement-precision result such as the lattice clock should rank below or above a discovery of new correlated physics; I have a bias toward the latter that I cannot fully separate from my own training in theory.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict with any shortlisted candidate or credited name is apparent from my profile; none of the credited people appears among my frequent co-authors or institutional ties. I withdraw my earlier B011 preference, which was an intellectual bias from my own work on machine learning for active matter and not a recusal; B011 is no longer in my configuration or alternatives. I share the Gothenburg physics environment with Johansson and Olsson and with Chalmers colleagues, with no specific collaboration with either.
